Where it began

Shadab Khan's story begins in Kamar Mushani, a town in Punjab's Mianwali district, where he was born on 4 October 1998. In 2008 his family moved to Rawalpindi, where he joined a local academy, the Bajwa Cricket Club, and then the Siddiq-e-Akbar Academy before being picked for Attock's under-19 side.

He soon caught the eye as a young leg-spinner who relied on flight and variety rather than pace, and his first Twenty20 match came for Rawalpindi in August 2016. That October he made 129 and took five wickets in an unofficial Test for Pakistan A in Bulawayo.

The player

He arrived in international cricket in a hurry. On his T20 debut against the West Indies in March 2017 he took three for 7 from four overs and was player of the match. His ODI and Test debuts followed within weeks, and that summer he was in the Pakistan side that won the Champions Trophy.

He played 6 Tests between 2017 and 2020, making 300 runs at 33.33 with three fifties and taking 14 wickets. His home was the shorter game: in March 2023 he became the first Pakistani man to take 100 T20 international wickets, and in October 2026 he made his first ODI hundred, an unbeaten 113 at the Gaddafi Stadium.

What made him special

He grew up admiring Shane Warne, and it showed in the way he gave the ball air and changed his angle on the crease. The googly got the headlines, but he always said the leg-break and the flipper took wickets too. In the field he was quick, bold and accurate, and he was counted among Pakistan's best fielders.

The batting took longer to bloom, and for a while he was seen as a bowler who could hit a bit. He set out to change that, and by 2026 he was being picked as a genuine all-rounder.

Away from the middle

In 2017 the PCB named him its Emerging Player of the Year. He captained Pakistan for the first time in a T20 international in 2020, and from 2021 he led Islamabad United in the PSL. At home in Punjabi, Urdu and English, he added a diploma in business management in 2025.

And finally

In that maiden ODI hundred he also shared an unbroken stand of 89 for the last wicket with Haris Rauf to win the game. It was a record for the last wicket in a successful ODI chase, and a fine way to celebrate a first hundred.
